newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's ONIC delivers warning on EU wheat storage.
newsitem.headline: France's ONIC delivers warning on EU wheat storage.

text.p: The European Union risks going back to the costly practice of buying unwanted wheat for intervention stores within months if it turns its back on exports, the head of France's ONIC grain authority said on Wednesday.

ONIC director general Alain Moulinier said the European Commisison had been "relatively generous" in the amount of wheat it had approved for export in December, but momentum would have to be maintained in the second half of the campaign.
"Whatever we don't export risks going into intervention and weighing on market prices," Moulinier told a news conference coinciding with the release of monthly supply/demand estimates.
Moulinier said the signs were some wheat would be added to intervention in Europe this year. But probably not in France, which was on the way to meeting its annual export goal.
The European Union has authorised soft wheat exports of 5.82 million tonnes so far this season, of which four million tonnes will apparently benefit French exporters, ONIC said.
ONIC has a 1996/97 (July/June) target of six million tonnes for commercial soft wheat exports to non-EU countries.
Moulinier said ONIC based the figure on zero intervention this year, with a projected carryout of 2.365 million tonnes giving the market about the right amount for operational needs.
"It depends on the export policy but I don't think there will be intervention in France this year," he said.

Moulinier argued the Uruguay Round global trade agreement left plenty of scope for exports in the second half of the campaign. But he acknowledged the EU was unlikely to reach its subsidised export quota this time despite a bumper 1996 harvest.
The pact allows the EU to export 18.2 million tonnes of wheat including durum and products with subsidies, of which Moulinier thought 15 to 16 million was a realistic target.

He reiterated European assertions that the Uruguay Round export quota is in theory much higher this year. The argument is that volumes that were exported without subsidy last year can be added to this year's allotment without breaking trade rules.

While that looks like an abstract dispute as long as the EU remains below its base export quota, European officials say it could cause fireworks with Washington near the end of the decade when demand might be strong enough to exceed the base amount.
U.S. officials have said the practice of piling up unused grain export quotas is against the spirit of the world trade agreement and might justify a legal challenge.
Not all French operators are as optimistic as Moulinier about exporting without resorting to intervention this year.
Traders said wheat prices have budged little since the end of 1996 because Europe's export opportunities are drying up with the arrival of new global supplies.
"It will be difficult to find new outlets. There is clearly going to be some in intervention," said one trader this week.
Others are worried about pressure on the EU farm budget in the wake of the mad cow crisis, saying export refunds are over budget and the EU might find it cheaper to store grain for now.
But Moulinier discounted this, saying intervention was a costly exercise and just deferred problems without solving them. --Tim Hepher, Paris newsroom +331 4221 5146
